speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. REGIER  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL CONCERNING MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I have in my hand an editorial, of which I sent you a copy, wherein, two weeks after a motion was decided by this house, you and with you the institution of parliament are still being attacked. To mention only a few of the terms used, you are referred to as "a crooked Speaker". You are compared to a bank robber. You are labelled "a selfseeking Liberal hack with the hide of a rhinoceros". You are accused of deliberately debasing an office.

To my mind this is an attack on our institution of parliament, and I am appealing to you, Mr. Speaker, to say whether some action cannot be taken to maintain or to restore, if it has been lost, public confidence in this institution.

subtopic: MR. REGIER  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL CONCERNING MR. SPEAKER
speechtext: Dissolve parliament.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. REGIER  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL CONCERNING MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
I am pleased to inform the hon. member that, according to a principle that has already been laid down and expounded in this house by other members who have risen on questions of privilege, an attack against the Speaker is an attack against the whole house. As a matter of fact, an attack against one member of the house is an attack against the whole house. See citation 157, Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition. Hon. members have risen from time to time on a question of privilege affecting the honour of a member of the house and have suggested or indicated that some action should be taken by myself. If the hon. member looks at May, fifteenth edition, he will find that whenever action has been taken it has never been by the Speaker but by members of the house themselves. See May's fifteenth edition, pages 125 and 126, also pages 138 to 142. You can find in May's fifteenth edition only one instance where the Speaker has acted himself, and that was when an officer of the house under his own jurisdiction had been attacked, and he came forward and submitted the matter to the house. In all other cases members have taken action themselves.
I must say that it has been quite some time since members have taken action with respect to these matters. The last instance took place some time ago. See Journals, page 108, 1894, and Journals, page 370, 1906. The proper procedure, which I explained myself on at least two previous occasions in the last month-see Hansard, 1956, pages 3563-6 and pages 4528-31-is that a member who wishes some action to be taken proceeds to indicate what constitutes the question of privilege and concludes with a motion. See Hansard, volume III, 1929, pages 2790-7, and Beauchesne's third edition, citation 273. That motion being privileged it may either be considered immediately or may be considered at a time appointed by the house itself. Once the motion has been agreed upon, if it is in order, then a remedy may be applied. That is entirely in the hands of the house and not in mine.
That remedy may consist of calling the author of the article or the publisher of the newspaper to the bar of the house and asking him for an explanation and apology. That apology or explanation may be accepted by the house. If it is not accepted, then the

house may decide whatever punishment it deems advisable. Then it calls back the author of the article or the publisher of the newspaper to the bar of the house, and it is the duty of the Speaker to communicate to him what decision the house has reached. That decision may be a reprimand; it may be imprisonment. In certain cases it has been advocated that even a fine may be decided upon. That was the case in Australia not very long ago. That is the way in which these matters should be looked upon.

subtopic: MR. REGIER  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL CONCERNING MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I speak to the point of order?
I should like to ask you if the hon. gentleman, before taking the formal action you have indicated, should not consider whether or not the criticisms he has read arise out of the incidents in this house upon which this house has already passed judgment. You will recall, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MR. REGIER  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL CONCERNING MR. SPEAKER
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member just to say that if a question of privilege is raised and it is not supported by a motion, there is nothing before the house and I would advise the hon. member not to pursue the point. He began by asking me a certain question. I would be pleased to tell him immediately that should that situation arise I shall have to deal with it when it comes up.

subtopic: MR. REGIER  REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER EDITORIAL CONCERNING MR. SPEAKER
speechtext: I am only asking you, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman should not take that into consideration before he takes the formal action that you have indicated. On a previous occasion you indicated that certain members of this house had used very extreme language with respect to the conduct of the officials of this house. It may be that this article would not go beyond the language that had been used in this house by some hon. members.

speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked a question with respect to the damage caused the supply ship C. D. Howe in Montreal on Sunday morning. There was damage done to about 15 or 20 tons of general cargo. The fire occurred in No. 2 deck area early Sunday morning, and was quickly brought under control. Loading operations had been completed for the dispatch of the vessel to northern areas when the fire broke out. The delay in sailing is one day, I am informed, and apparently no damage has been done other than to the 15 tons of general cargo. None of the mail has been disturbed and the rest of the cargo is intact, so there will be only a slight delay in the vessel leaving Montreal.

The house resumed, from Monday, June 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Harris for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

subtopic: SUPPLY SHIP "C. D. HOWE"-REPORT ON FIRE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I rose last evening and attempted to adjourn the debate at five minutes to ten I felt that I was in a position somewhat similar to that of the hon. member for Broadview on Friday, when he attempted to adjourn the debate at ten minutes to six. I, of course, wanted to do some research and gather more material. I suspect the hon. member for Broadview wanted to let the Prime Minister age another couple of hours so he would have something to talk about.

subtopic: SUPPLY SHIP "C. D. HOWE"-REPORT ON FIRE
speechtext: That is pretty flat.

subtopic: SUPPLY SHIP "C. D. HOWE"-REPORT ON FIRE
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) would have filled in, but I was not disposed to accept his kind offer. When the Leader of the Opposition introduced the motion which


we are now debating he used these words, as found on page 5330 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, on a supply motion it is particularly appropriate-
I want you to note the word "appropriate," Mr. Speaker.
-at this time that I should refer to the discussions that have already taken place here and their effect upon our present position in this house. I think it is the correct time to express our belief that this government has lost any moral right to govern this country.
I say at this point that if there has been any immorality in action during this session in this house it has been on the part of the official opposition. The Leader of the Opposition went on to say:
We all know how precedents were broken in this house in a debate which took place not long ago. There was some discussion on Friday last about whether or not the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had used the words in a television interview, "We violated the rules''.
I am sure if the Minister of Trade and Commerce said anything of that nature what he meant to say was, "We violated no rules"; or he meant to say, and should have said, "We applied the rules". The opposition do not seem to be able to see any difference between applying the rules and violating the rules. The Leader of the Opposition went on for over half a page and discussed proceedings in this house with respect to the rules and sought to indicate that the government, and the government only, had violated the rules. He said further, on page 5331:
I am not going to say more except to repeat that the important thing is not that he did say the words; the important thing is that having said them he denied to this house that he did. It is only in keeping with many of the things that have happened.
All this is an attempt by the Leader of the Opposition to justify the motion he has brought before the house to dissolve the house. So far as his comments are concerned, that was as far as he went. Then he proceeded to attack the other place.
It has been said in the debate on the question to which he referred earlier, namely the debate on the pipe line, that the remarks have not been relevant and have been off the normal course of debate. I do not believe this party can be accused of such a type of debate. The opposition have tried to indicate that we have attacked the rules of the house and that we are undermining the pillars of democracy. From what has taken place so far I know that the Leader of the Opposition and the opposition generally, because they have been unable to force their will upon the majority, have moved on to a smaller group, the officials of the house, and have attempted to destroy

them. That was not possible, and they have now moved on to the Senate and have attempted to destroy the other place. If there are destroyers of parliamentary and democratic systems in this house they are on the benches on the other side of the house.

pipe-line bill, we can speak on all the projects which are of interest to the maritime provinces-

I say immediately that I know the difficulty of the position because of certain pronouncements that were made. That does not alter the fact that the rules are exactly as I have stated. We are not supposed to refer to or reflect upon past proceedings.
There were proceedings in a certain debate which has ended. As a matter of fact the legislation that was then under discussion has become the law of the land. There were also proceedings that took place on Thursday, May 31, and Friday, June 1, which, as the hon. member knows, consisted in large part of a motion of censure against myself, which has also been voted by the house on June 8. I realize the difficulty, and I do not mind at all, as far as I am concerned, if hon. members generally wish to have the rules dispensed with in respect to this particular debate. In citation 107 of Beauchesne's third edition I find the following:
In all matters of doubt, the Speaker will consider attentively the opinions of members of experience, or sometimes, instead of expressing his opinion on either side, may ask instructions from the house or reserve his decision on the point in discussion, or suggest that the house may, if it think proper, dispense with the rule in a particular case. In doubtful cases, he will be largely guided by circumstances.
If hon. members insist on discussing previous proceedings already disposed of, I am in their hands and they may make their own decision.

The motion before us is one to dissolve the house. The only real argument that has been put up by the official opposition as to why we should dissolve the house is that undoubtedly they could win a general election. One is what we believe to be an excellent arrangement with the provinces for a tax-rental agreement; another is provision for assistance to unemployed who do not otherwise receive assistance under the Unemployment Insurance Act. There are many pieces of legislation that are of importance to the country.
I think the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the C.C.F. party should take these under consideration, rather than attempt to do something which will be particularly beneficial to their own political parties.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the 17-year Liberal nightmare in my province which ended in 1952 the Liberal party lost no opportunity to broadcast with fervour that New Brunswick was indeed Canada's unspoiled province by the sea. The Liberal governments with which New Brunswick had been plagued for 17 long, miserable years lifted nary a finger to provide opportunities for our people in that hitherto barren and hard-scrabble land which was New Brunswick. But New Brunswick had become by 1952, as was confirmed by the Prime Minister in two recent statements, the most backward and most depressed area of Canada.
The Prime Minister did not stop to think that these very Atlantic provinces of which New Brunswick is a part, economically speaking and developmentwise, were saddled for the past 20 years-with the exception of New Brunswick alone-not only provincially but federally with Liberal governments. If the maritime provinces are the most backward provinces in Canada we have no one to blame but the Liberal governments that sat in those provinces and in this house during that time.
However, in 1952 New Brunswick changed governments. Hugh John Flemming and his administration have succeeded in reversing the downward economic trend that existed in our province for 50 years and we look forward to a new era, a new day, when progress and prosperity will replace the continuous economic depression with which we were saddled, and the dispersion of our


industry; and the dispersal of our young people, driven from our shores to the long-Conservative province of Ontario in order to make a living.
But while our provincial government in New Brunswick is doing all it can to make New Brunswick the province it was destined to become in the Canadian federation, let us remember that the federal government is not doing its share and has never accepted its responsibilities toward the maritime provinces. Alas, Mr. Speaker, this attitude of the federal Liberal government toward the Atlantic provinces in the past 20 years has been one of neglect, laziness, indifference and downright cowardice.
The federal government has been steadily and actively selling the Atlantic provinces down the river. The federal government has never varied in its stupid and traitorous attitude of passiveness, laziness and indifference toward the stark fact that until we in this economic entity comprising the maritime provinces can adopt, adjust and enforce trade conditions and regulations to meet our needs and not only those of central Canada; until we can decide and determine ourselves how and where we will buy, sell, export and import; until we can regain our natural markets; until we can develop enough hydroelectric power to compete with the rates charged in other areas in Canada; until we can decide and determine ourselves how and where we will buy, sell, export and import; until we can regain the same advantageous trade position we enjoyed at the time of confederation in regard to our choice of buying and selling markets and our method of transportation, which was then mainly by water; and until we can overcome our power, transportation and market barriers, we are doomed to remain a lopsided economic entity, discarded by a federal government which is too blind to see the forest for the trees and which has been-whether or not it has enough brains to realize it-persistently selling the Atlantic provinces down the river.
How I was taken aback the other day by a statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he mentioned that he had become enthusiastic about the pipe-line bill to the apparent extent that he was prepared to sell parliament down the road of dictatorship and sell the liberty of its members in order to bulldoze through this house a loan of $80 million to permit a United States company to have control.

One trouble with this government is that its Minister of Trade and Commerce will not get off his high horse to examine and recognize the horrible conditions his government has permitted to exist and develop in the maritime provinces. Mr. Speaker, the present Liberal government has no idea of what we need or what we require or what we want. It is blind and cannot see. It is weak and cannot walk. It is deaf and will not hear. It is lazy and will not work. It is indifferent and will not act. It fails to recognize the fundamental principle that indifference leads to death. Pilate was indifferent to the fate of Christ, and Christ ended by dying upon a cross. Indifference leads but to ruin. Indifference is the companion of chaos, and indifference toward the maritime provines is the main characteristic of the present federal Liberal government.
New Brunswick is now embarking upon a tremendous program of hydroelectric development. The first phase of the program is the Beechwood project, which will cost about $45 million. But the over-all program for hydroelectric power development on the Saint John river comprises four projects like Beechwood and will cost over $211 million. Yet in spite of the federal government giving $162 million to the Colombo plan to help develop projects like Beechwood in Pakistan; in spite of the federal government bulldozing through parliament this $80 million loan; in spite of the $4,044,200,000 lent or given away in the past few years to foreign countries- but mostly given away-many of them behind the iron curtain, this federal Liberal government refuses to endorse our note for $45 million to help us build Beechwood.
The answer given by the Prime Minister was that we did not need money; our finances were good. In making this statement the Prime Minister missed the point entirely. We could borrow the money, and we did. Our finances were solid because since 1952 we have had a Conservative government which reestablished them. But, Mr. Speaker, in wishing to get the endorsement of the federal government for this loan we wanted to save

538S
Request for Election and Senate Reform the difference between the high rate of interest we have to pay without the federal government's endorsement and the rate we would have to pay with it. On the $211 million the difference in interest will be costing New Brunswick something like $3 million a year. This $3 million a year is what the government of New Brunswick wanted to save.
Furthermore, by saving this amount per year on the interest rate we would be in a position to offer rates on power coming from the Saint John river projects which would be much lower, and thus New Brunswick would be in a better position to compete with power rates charged in the other provinces of Canada. Those are the reasons this endorsement was requested from the federal government. There was no question that we could not borrow the money. There was no question about our finances. It was merely to give us a chance to save some money without costing the taxpayers of Canada 5 cents. It would not have affected the monetary position of Canada in the least. It would have merely given us the opportunity to develop our electric power cheaply and sell it at a much better rate.
Now let us pass to another example of what I would call a downright traitorous attitude toward the Atlantic provinces. The federal Liberal government has refused to build the Chignecto canal, giving the ill-thought out excuse that there is not sufficient need for that canal to build it now. Let me tell this house that if sufficient need does not now exist it is precisely because the federal Liberal government, by its stupidity, has driven those industries out of the maritimes which hitherto depended upon cheap water transportation to the main markets. The lack of cheap transportation is one of the main reasons why our industries, one after another, have been forced to close their doors, forced to the wall by the stupidity of a federal government which will not recognize our continually mounting transportation charges.
Before confederation our natural buying and selling markets were supplied by water, that is by cheap transportation. Confederation removed those markets but promised to bring about conditions in the Atlantic provinces which would permit us to trade profitably in the confederation-made markets of central Canada. Thus, like trying to change the course of the St. Lawrence river itself, confederation tried to make us change our natural trade routes. First came the tall tariff barriers, which removed our natural buying and selling markets to the east and to the south. Then came the mounting transportation costs which did not take into account

the guaranteed freight rate differential promised by confederation. As a result we were choked and forced to the wall. Today many of our remaining industries, like Enterprise foundries in Sackville to recall only one, stay in the maritimes only because of a spirit of service and loyalty to the people of the maritime provinces. A location nearer to the confederation-made markets of central Canada would be much more profitable for them.
At the time of confederation it was recognized that the maritimes might gain advantages which would overcome the disadvantages resulting from the removal of our natural trade markets. We had that advantage, and could still have it in cheap transportation by water. In this connection the need for the Chignecto canal was recognized and the building of a ship's railway was undertaken but never completed. Now that power is coming to New Brunswick, industries are looking in our province for sites on which to establish themselves. So long as this federal government keeps killing our industries by "nickeling" us to death with ever increasing transportation costs, with staggering freight rates, and by using every possible device to increase those freight rates, industrial growth in New Brunswick will be stilted and our people will not share equally in the wealth which Canada offers.
Transportation is a federal matter. The Chignecto canal and the building of our much needed ports like Dalhousie, Jacquet River and Saint John, would permit the establishment of numerous industries because cheaper water transportation would be provided. Public statements have been made by leading industrialists in New Brunswick that refineries would be built if the Chignecto canal were built. The Chignecto canal would open up cheap routes to coastwise shipping, to all points east and to the markets to be served by the St. Lawrence seaway. No sooner would the canal be built than the once great need for the canal would become apparent and real again, for the new era of industrial development which has been commenced in New Brunswick would be augmented and given new impetus. The federal government is responsible if the present need for the canal has in part been removed, and it is responsible so long as it does not build this canal to restore that need and fulfil a promise made at the time of confederation.
Now let us look at the new increase in freight rates. Even before the commission decided on the merits of another increase, and before the evidence was presented to back up this new demand, an interim increase of 7 per cent was allowed. When

is this government going to stop "nickeling" us to death in the maritimes? This increase is just another example of the contempt for the maritime provinces. But, Mr. Speaker, we know the real reason the government is denying us our right to the Chignecto canal. We know this government is blocking progress in the maritimes in order to keep the Canadian National as the only means of transportation. Does anyone think they can make our people swallow this ridiculous premise and pay the staggering freight rates which are being charged? This government knows that new industries would more than offset the possible but not probable slight, temporary lessening of freight business on the Canadian National if the maritimes were given a chance to prosper and develop by placing at their disposal cheap transportation by water and by rail.
I do not need to explain the guarantees given to the maritimes through the British North America Act, or at the time of confederation, for preferential freight rates to permit us to compete in the confederation-made markets which were forced upon us. Let me say this. This federal Liberal government has not recognized this guarantee and has done nothing to offset the ruinous position in which we are now. On the one hand we are prevented from dealing with our old buying and selling markets because of trade barriers and tariffs. On the other hand we are being denied a competitive trading position because of killing transportation costs to the confederation-made markets of central Canada.
We are blocked no matter which way we turn. We are caught in the vise of federal Liberal indifference. I, for one, am on the verge of crying out, like Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland, "Give us a square deal or count us out". Stop selling us down the river or get out of the way and let us look after our own affairs to our own best interests. Stop killing us, or make road for us to pass. It is a fortunate thing for us that the next elections are not far away, for as soon as this country gets the government it deserves, a Conservative government under the indomitable leadership of our leader, we will have a new deal and justice will be done to the Atlantic provinces for the first time in our history.
What else but laziness, indifference and apathy prevent the federal government from taking steps to bring about the building of that Campbellton-Cross Point bridge about which the Prime Minister encouraged us to talk five years ago? The Minister of Public Works himself has mentioned to me the enthusiastic letters he received from the premier of my province demanding the bridge, 67509-341

It would be a tremendous defence asset, for the only link between Quebec and New Brunswick at the present time is that old, antiquated Matapedia bridge which threatens to collapse every spring and fall. Quebec farmers would find ready markets, and there would be an interchange of commerce which has never existed between our two provinces. The truckers of pulpwood to our mills would be greatly helped, not to mention the great opportunities we would have to use for transportation the new good roads of New Brunswick and Quebec.
The ferry service is most inadequate; it is outdated, a time killer; it is a danger every spring and fall. The bridge would cost hardly more than $1 million, which the Minister of Trade and Commerce says is nothing. The Sugar Loaf mountain, which contains millions of tons of solid rock, could be had for the asking to build the solid stretches of the bridge, and a comparatively small steel span is all that would be needed in the middle.
"What's a million dollars?", says the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Let me tell him that it is more than we ever got from this government, in my riding, until this year. This is, of course, also excepting the $100,000 or so the federal Liberals put into Madawaska county to try to defeat the Conservative candidates in the last election. This was the first sign of federal assistance we ever got in Madawaska, and it is too bad that it came in the form of gin, whisky, nylon stockings and boxes of chocolates. But our people were far too intelligent to sell their right to vote for gin or nylon stockings, and the Liberal candidates got what they deserved, a well earned and well merited defeat.
The position of this government is ridiculous in regard to the maritime provinces. I repeat what I have often said. A few men are running this country, supported by this tremendous Liberal majority. This government gives me the impression that it is running a school for trained seals, and so long as the Liberal members keep on acting like trained seals, bowing subserviently up and down for the herring held before their noses, they can expect to get the famous S.S.S., that great title in Liberal political life, the safe seat somewhere. For this long-sought S.S.S. and more and more election slush funds, they sell their constituents down the river. This has been the characteristic hallmark of Liberal representation by maritime Liberal members in this house. But by their silence and inactive conduct they give the erroneous impression that all is well in the maritimes.

The Prime Minister has on two occasions now, once in his letter of January 14, 1955, and in his statement in Toronto at the convention some months ago, indicated in no uncertain terms the recognition by his government of the plight of the maritime provinces. This federal government, with the Minister of Labour sitting idly by, has on the one hand recognized the need for financial help and with the other hand has kept on slapping the maritimes in the face, as it has been slapping us in the face for the past 20 years.
Our Senate is hardly anything any more. It is just another S. S. S., another safe seat somewhere for Liberal politicians. It is the hallmark of Liberal service. Thus we have a Senate packed by old Liberal stand-bys and money-hungry buccaneers who are often in their dotage when they reach the Senate and merely act as a rubber stamp for whatever measures may be sent to it. It has become a tarnished badge of respectability for the whims of the government big-wigs in their puerile efforts to cover up their sinful inefficiency. We have no room in our democracy for such an expensive rubber stamp.
Certainly if we are to provide Canada with the government it deserves we must make the Senate a legislative body representative of the wishes of the people. This would only be brought about by an elective Senate, or in part an elective Senate. Let the Senators be responsible to the people who would elect them, and not be appointed to anoint with the cloak of respectability such legislation as the infamous pipe-line bill. Had we had a responsible, independent Senate, debate would not have been curtailed, and the Liberal members of the Senate would not have had to make the statements they did.
The need for Senate reform has been recognized by all leaders of all political parties, but so far the government has not shown the courage needed to call a conference of the provinces to deal with this very long-overdue reform. This is just another pitiable example of Liberal neglect.
It is most unfortunate, but there is one bright picture on the horizon as far as my province is concerned. I learned yesterday that the rat-infested station and freight shed at Edmundston will be replaced in 1957 and that the plans have now been completed. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Transport for having answered this request. Nevertheless I wish to say this. The jumping, squirming, flipper-flapping jack in the box, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, could very well hightail back to the squid-jigging grounds of Newfoundland and help some poor fisherman bail out his boat. He would be more useful there than he is in this house.


There is one thing I wish to bring out at this time. I just returned from my riding. Some messenger from the Department of Labour, a Mr. Bosse, got up and made the statement at Edmundston before some Liberal assembly that there never would be a new station at Edmundston. He said, "Regardless of what the government wants to do, I am going to block it." Mr. Speaker, it has got to a sad point in the history of this country when messengers of the minister and his department are going to tell the people of this country what the government is going to do and what parliament is here for.
It is apparent that the federal government refuses to recognize the financial position which has been imposed by confederation upon New Brunswick, either through a refusal to learn the facts or because of a subversive attitude toward the government of the province of New Brunswick. Either reason, or a combination of both reasons, place the choking problem right on the doorstep of New Brunswick's representative in the government, the Minister of Labour. Either he has acquiesced where he should have spoken up and fought for the province, or he acted in unison with men like the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) in their expressed determination to block progress in my province merely because the people of my province had the good sense to throw out that decadent Liberal government in 1952 and replace it with the leadership we now have.
The Minister of Labour knew and was aware of the government policy, as stated in the Prime Minister's letter of January 14, 1955, which reads:
The present government has no intention of abandoning the objective of the tax rental agreements which is to make it financially possible for all the provinces whatever their tax base to perform their constitutional functions themselves and to provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation.
We agree with this statement of policy. But here is where the Minister of Labour should have intervened with effectiveness. By the letters of the Prime Minister of January 6, 1956, and January 18, 1956, New Brunswick is being denied the right-and this was confirmed by the Prime Minister at the last interprovincial conference-to provide a reasonable level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation. I have the figures here, with the schedules for all the taxes New Brunswick is forced to impose, and they prove conclusively that the over-all level of the New Brunswick tax rate is substantially higher than in any other province. Our premier, Hon. Hugh John

Flemming, submitted to the last interprovincial conference schedules and tabulations which prove that the burden of taxation in New Brunswick is the most onerous of any province in Canada.
In relation to the personal income of the people of New Brunswick, figures for 1953 show that our people had to pay 41 per cent more in taxes out of personal income than the average Canadian. Again we hold the Minister of Labour responsible for endorsing a federal government which keeps in the vise of federal indifference and antagonism the very province he is appointed to represent. I should like to quote an observation by our premier during the last interprovincial conference, when he said:
It is an essential requirement of any provincial government to so manage its affairs that the credit of the province is maintained on a sound basis. This is particularly true for a province in the position of New Brunswick which at the moment is faced with very substantial, indeed I might say staggering, capital expenditures for the development of electric generating facilities, both hydro and thermal, to meet the needs of the new mining developments, the expansion of the pulp and paper industry and to provide the power required for the increase in service and secondary industries which these developments will normally bring in their train.

I should like to take the opportunity of speaking shortly on this motion because I have a few ideas I should like to express that have been disturbing not only me but many members of the public in connection with the type of opposition that is being met with by this government in this house.
I read over the speech of the Leader of the Opposition today and I listened very carefully yesterday when he spoke, with a view to ascertaining exactly what the grounds were on which he supported this motion that the Prime Minister dissolve this house immediately and call an election as soon as possible.
The foremost ground put forward by the Leader of the Opposition, without referring to details of the recent gas pipe-line debate, is that the Speaker of this house and the Deputy Speaker and deputy chairman of committees were dominated by the government in this house and that their position has been called into question. Under the ruling that the Speaker has given, it is not permissible for me to refer to details of that debate, and I shall refrain from doing so. I simply want to make the observation that it is my firm conviction that any person reading that debate could come to no other conclusion but that the officials of this house whose position has been challenged acted honourably and impartially and free from any pressure by this government.
I also point out to the house that nobody has called into question the position of the officials of this house except the official opposition. It would be an absurd position if this house were in the position where, because the opposition calls into question the conduct of the officials of this house-and I may say, sir, calls them into question improperly-they could therefore, upon the basis of that demand, feel justified in obtaining an election.
The second ground advanced by the Leader of the Opposition is that a member of the cabinet, the representative of the government in the other place, has bent to the will of this government in the discharge of his duties in the other place and that he has procured the other members of the house to bend to the will of this government. I point out to the house that the Leader of the Opposition has not adduced the slightest evidence to substantiate such a charge. It is


difficult for me to realize how a man could be in public life as long as he has and make serious charges of that kind without endeavouring to persuade this house in the slightest degree that the charges are substantiated by adducing any evidence to this house.
I am not permitted to refer to the debates that took place in the other place, and I do not intend to do so, but I want to say that from talking to people who heard those debates their reaction was that the other place could reach no other conclusion but that the gas pipe-line bill should be approved, and approved expeditiously.
The Leader of the Opposition has urged that this government has lost the moral right to govern this country. I say that that is simply not true. This government did nothing in the gas pipe-line debate and in the applying of closure that it was not entitled to do and that was not completely proper, and the people of this country are wholeheartedly still in favour of the present government continuing to administer the affairs of this country.
The last accusation of the Leader of the Opposition is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce bent this house to his will. This is another type of charge which it is difficult to meet, as many charges are when accusations of this kind are made, but it is completely untrue.
I point out to this house that the whole cabinet supported the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Eight members of the cabinet spoke in support of this resolution and the subsequent bill, and I estimate that about 60 members from the government side did so. I know that hon. members from time to time make light of the support given by backbenchers on this side to measures of the government. I ask them in all sincerity if it is not the practice in Canadian politics for members of every party to support their own party in so far as their conscience permits them to do so. I have not made a check on the debates and proceedings in this house, but I dare say that if a check were made it would show that the members of the C.C.F. party and the Conservative party support their leaders to just as great an extent as the members of this party support the government. I can tell them that, in connection with the gas pipe line, there was no doubt whatsoever about the sentiments of this party. They were wholeheartedly in favour of it because they believed that the gas pipe-line bill was a good thing and they realized that the only way of putting a bill through and having the majority express its wishes in this house was by the application of closure.

The matter that somewhat disturbs me and is disturbing to many other people in this country is what I describe as the evil tendency of the opposition to denigrate and belittle and attack the integrity of men who are occupying prominent positions in this government and this country. I simply point to this motion. The basis of the attack in this case is against the three officials of this house and against the government leader in the other place and, indirectly, against all members in that other place and against the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In any country this would be a serious enough thing, but this is not a sporadic, unpremeditated episode. It is part of a systematic attempt on the part of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) to undermine public confidence in the integrity of the men who are directing the affairs of this government. When I say it is not something unpremeditated and that it is a systematic attempt, I need only refer to what has happened in this parliament on other occasions. I will not go into the particulars of the debates because I do not want to transgress against the rules, but I point out that the same type of attack has been levelled against the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in connection with the debate on external affairs. He was accused of not being candid with parliament. I consider that an attack upon his integrity. He was accused of withholding information that the house was entitled to receive.
But there has recently been some little change of direction in the attack upon the Prime Minister of this country. The reason must be perfectly obvious. It must be realized that with the ordinary men and women of Canada his reputation is beyond reproach. As a result we see some of the second lieutenants called into action such as the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) who made a speech the other night in which he referred to the Prime Minister as being old and tired. On what basis? Because he only participated about four or five times in the gas pipe line debate. That may indicate weariness and lack of interest to some members of the opposition but I will tell you what it indicates to the public. The people of Canada believe that the Prime Minister of this country was too much of a gentleman, too much of a statesman, to stoop to lower himself to the political gutter because the Leader of the Opposition did in the pipe line debate.

Yesterday the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Gardiner) endeavoured to give some reasons why he did not think it would be a wise thing to go to the people at this time, and I believe he more or less inadvertently gave the clue to the reluctance of himself, the government and their supporters to go to the people at this time. He said in one part of his speech that in his opinion certain things that had been said by the opposition were not properly understood by the public, and then he said: "Just give them a few weeks and then we will see what the people will say." Apparently he feels there is something that he wants the public to forget because he wants to give them a few

weeks, or better still, a few months, and then go to the public. That indicates that the government is anxious that the people should forget certain things that have taken place. So far as the real issues are concerned, I propose today to give five reasons why I believe it would be proper and appropriate for this house to be dissolved and to go to the country at this time or in the nearest possible future.
The burden of the reply to this motion by the Liberal speakers so far has been the claim of prosperity. Again and again they have repeated that this country is experiencing the greatest prosperity in its history. Mr. Speaker, I think there is something a little bit rude-if I might use that word- about that kind of a boast made in this house. I should like to read to them a bit of scripture. I am sure they will not mind my doing so. I should like to refer them to the fortieth verse of the twenty-fifth chapter of St. Matthew, which reads as follows:
40 And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Why do I quote that passage of scripture? Because when they make these boasts about prosperity, they back up their arguments by pointing to the business world, to the increased dividends being paid by the huge corporations, and to the huge profits that are being reaped by the huge corporations in this country. To them that constitutes prosperity. But to me, Mr. Speaker, and, I am sure, to my colleagues in this party and to a great many people in this country, many of whom at present are in the class who may not be even supporters of this party but who are of a sympathetic nature politically speaking, prosperity does not mean huge profits or huge dividends to the shareholders of our corporations. Prosperity means the well-being and the welfare of every citizen in this country. As long as there is one citizen in this country who through no fault of his own or her own is suffering, we cannot claim that we have achieved prosperity in this country. There are many hundreds of thousands-yes, perhaps millions-in this country who are today not experiencing anything like the prosperity we heard talked about by members on the government side of this house.
Even a quick look at the statistics will indicate that the average income of the families in this country is a long way from being such that they are in the position in which they can buy even the essentials of life such as the food, clothing and shelter which they require. Then of course we have the whole sector of our economy which comes under the general description of agriculture. Members
26, 1956	5405
Request for Election and Senate Reform on both sides of the house but particularly members on the Liberal side of it have admitted from time to time that, whereas we have this so-called prosperity, our agricultural section of the country has not shared in that prosperity. As a matter of fact, in the last few years, it has been getting a smaller share of the national income than before. How can members supporting the government say that this country is experiencing prosperity when the most important basic industry in this country upon which our whole economy is based has been experiencing a severe recession in recent years? How can members of the government say that all is well, that there is no need for a reference to the people, and that this government should carry on in its merry way, when they know that that part of our population which is engaged in agriculture is now receiving the smallest share of the national income, in proportion to its numbers, that it has received since 1933 when we were at the depth of the depression? Those are facts and figures they must face.
That is why I say it is a little bit rude and boastful to be talking about this prosperity when there are thousands, hundreds of thousands and perhaps millions of people in this country who are not enjoying what is known as prosperity but who are struggling to make ends meet. There are many thousands who are living at a substandard level or a subsubsistence level in this country. You have only to contact the welfare societies across this country and the various organizations which are interested in the welfare of the people, and they will point out to you people living in poverty, in hunger, practically in starvation in our midst, while we talk about prosperity and the members supporting the government use that as an argument or a reason why they should not go to the people at this time. I therefore say that my first reason why this motion should carry and why a reference should be made to the public at this time is that this government has failed agriculture. It has failed agriculture in several ways. I will mention two in particular.
First of all, I want to associate myself with the remarks made by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) with regard to freight rates. Certainly the government has not protected the interests of agriculture by allowing freight rates to go hopscotching on their way year after year. Let me say this. The hon. member for Bow River has already drawn attention to the fact that one of the companies-that is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company-without taking into account profits which they get from their mining interests, hotels and other interests

Request for Election and Senate Reform but out of their transportation alone, accumulated a profit of $37J million.
It may be argued that the Canadian National Railways from time to time require money because they have a deficit. I want to make it perfectly clear that there is a great difference between giving assistance to the Canadian National Railways and giving assistance to the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not think a flat increase across the board in freight rates is the right way in which to come to the assistance of the Canadian National Railways. Certainly the Canadian Pacific Railway does not require it. The Canadian National Railways is partly if not totally owned by the Canadian people. We have an interest in it. We have a stake in it. We rescued several bankrupt private companies and formed them into a national railway system. That railway system is there to serve the people of Canada. It was not intended or designed to be a profit-making organization. Certainly we are happy and glad to see a surplus if they can operate efficiently and revenues are buoyant enough. We are glad to see the Canadian National Railways make a surplus. But that is not the reason why the Canadian National Railways was established in this country. It was established to provide service.
You have only to look at the map of Canada, particularly one of western Canada, to see the reason why the Canadian National Railways has a financial struggle as compared with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Here is a railway that had to run branch lines or spur lines into the most uneconomic parts of the prairie west, when the west was opening up, in order to provide a service-often at a loss-so that people would not be left isolated in communities without service. They were put there to provide service whereas the C.P.R. would not touch it with a ten-rod pole. For that reason the C.N.R. have had to suffer deficits. Any time that the Canadian National Railway system can show that they require a grant of money from this parliament or some form of assistance in order to provide a greater service for the Canadian people, I for one would be glad to vote such assistance. To lump them together with the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is nothing but a purely commercial profit-making organization, and to say that because we have to give some assistance to the Canadian National Railways, we will raise the freight rates across the board and let this huge Canadian Pacific Railway system benefit also is going about the matter in the wrong way and doing it to the detriment of agriculture.
The government has also failed the farmer in a very important principle with regard

In the last three or four years- and as a matter of fact, more than that, but more recently it has been given greater emphasis among farm organizations-my colleagues and I in this house and others have been fighting for the principle of parity prices for agriculture. Mr. Speaker, we are in the 22nd parliament of Canada which normally should run for a five-year period. At the three-year point we find ourselves confronted with a motion of non-confidence in the government moved by the opposition and it is based on moral reasons rather than on legal reasons. This is an unusual procedure, to say the least; and we must examine into the circumstances surrounding the debate on the establishment of Canada's first natural gas pipe line in order to consider what underlies the situation. However, I think it is only necessary to say that in that debate the government enforced the rule of law to the distaste of the opposition, based as it is on Magna Carta and the British North America Act. In particular we enforced in this chamber that rule which is based on the common ordinary phrase "majority rule".
[Mr. Dufresne.l

To come down to the procedure in this house, the rule which was enforced was that the house is master of its own procedure in times of emergency as existed during that debate. If the government is immoral, Mr. Speaker, we should like to know the particulars. However, I think it follows, if the government is immoral because of what it has done in enforcing the rule of law, that we are in company with Premier Frost of Ontario whose support we had here, and in company with Premier Manning of Alberta and Premier Campbell of Manitoba.

subtopic: SUPPLY SHIP "C. D. HOWE"-REPORT ON FIRE

But going abroad at this time, there are deliberations taking place within the sphere of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and I say to this house that if the government is immoral so is a very prominent member of the government, one who has certainly been honoured by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and has been praised and named in the public press of the world, as one of "the three wise men" in NATO. So at this time we find with regret, the opposition reflecting upon one of our most eminent Canadians as he goes abroad to reorganize and reorientate the functions of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. That is a strange situation. But we look forward to a reorganized NATO for better world trade and for better economic conditions. If NATO can be used for war prevention, it can be used for peaceful pursuits such as better trade and better economic conditions throughout the world. We are proud of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), past president of United Nations as he is, and we wish him well despite the domestic wrangle fomented by the opposition at this time on the home front.
However, I wonder about this matter of morality in public affairs, Mr. Speaker. We have noticed of late how queer it is that Her Majesty's loyal opposition, so firm in their moral position in this debate, boycott the ceremony of royal assent as we obtain assent to the legislation which has been passed by this house. Indeed, can we not say that their morals are a little bit weak on commonwealth relations, and matters affecting the crown so near and dear to us all?

before the house and I say it is a similar story which underlies the motion of non-confidence concerning the Speaker of this house. In my view, there is a new outlook as to sportsmanship on the part of the opposition because we can sum up their activities in this way: If you lose a game, attack the referee and the umpire and the officials; then you will feel better. This is indeed a new code of sportsmanship. But we see emanating from the other side of the house likewise a new code of political morals based on national disunity, minority rule and freedom of speech run rampant. Indeed, I see this once famous party which was the party of the fathers of confederation presenting to Canada in these months in this parliament a retrogressive Conservative new deal for Canada. Shades of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Robert Borden! If the day comes when we shall be unveiling a statue of Sir Robert Borden on parliament hill, I wonder how members opposite will be able to go and attend that ceremony for that great man, who was indeed a leader in the field of national unity.
I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal in January, 1956, reporting the proceedings of the Progressive Conservative party in Canada, and reporting an event which took place in the presence of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and other top-ranking dignitaries of the party. On that occasion an address was delivered by Mr. Grattan O'Leary editor of the Ottawa Journal and he laid down, as do so many members of the party opposite, a policy for the party in his own way. I wish to quote in part as follows. He said to the party chieftains and the party followers on that occasion:
Our task is to mobilize the spirit of discontent and channel it into support of the Conservative party and the people know we are the only alternative.
This indeed is a fine sounding policy for the successors to the fathers of confederation. As they sow, so shall they reap; and generally, if they are going to rely on disunity and discontent, that is what they will reap. One need only turn to the province of Quebec in order to see what has happened to the Conservative party there. It is practically extinct, save and except for the remnants which remain by way of alliance with Premier Duplessis, based as they are on supernationalism. We can look to the prairies and British Columbia. In that great part of the country Conservatives are not even an alternative; they are not even a desperate alternative. What are we to say of their position with Premier Frost, that great premier of Ontario who took a forthright stand on Canada's

On this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, we of the Liberal party have more things to do for Canada than to think about politics and elections at this time. We wish to see a better division of the tax revenues as between Ottawa and the provinces. This is a matter which will come before this chamber in due course. Perhaps at this session good results will come from the solution of this longstanding problem now that we have worked towards a better division of revenues than ever for the good of Canada. We wish to see brought before this house legislation which will enable unemployment assistance to be shared by the dominion and the provinces to cover those unemployed not covered by unemployment insurance. In addition, we believe that the government will bring before the house, before this session concludes, legislation to cover better unemployment insurance for those now entitled to it under the statute. Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is in the process of negotiation as between this government and the provinces the matter of health insurance proposals. Those proposals are of vital interest to the nation. They stand to be implemented and the optimistic spirit which prevails is at an all-time high. We look forward to stage one in the national health insurance before long. We look forward to nation-wide hospital insurance as a result.
Now, let me deal with the dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements briefly. This rearrangement of tax revenues could mean more revenue and better opportunities to fulfil provincial obligations in so far as the citizens of the provinces are concerned. In particular, I am one who looks forward in Ontario to better old age pensions for our senior citizens following upon these fiscal rearrangements. Every member in this house knows that in Ontario now the old age pension is up to $60 at age 65 by reason of joint co-operation between this government and the province. However, I must say that the top figure, $60, is only made available after the application of a very rigid provincial-municipal means test. I think of that great province of ours, Ontario, the industrial giant that it is and greater it will become, but I think it does not stand up by way of comparison in what it is doing for the old age pensioners when we compare what takes place in some of the western provinces. Therefore, I for one would

I feel, too, that we can always at the federal level look forward to improving our pension legislation because in my city of Toronto there is much need amongst the pensioners. We must constantly be thinking of their needs and problems. They are our senior citizens. In particular, I wish to say a word about pensions for new Canadians. This involves the problem of obtaining more suitable immigrants overseas. If Canada is to succeed in this mid-twentieth century she must have good immigrants from places where immigrants will be found who are suitable to the political and economic needs of Canada. I mention the United Kingdom and I mention Europe. Those places are sources of immigrants, but they are places where old age security is a paramount problem and where good measures exist for those entitled to old age security. How can we expect the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) to obtain suitable immigrants in great numbers for Canada if when they arrive here they have to wait 20 years before being entitled to old age assistance or security? I think, Mr. Speaker, what the government should consider in due course, perhaps at the next session, would be a provision that after a new Canadian becomes a citizen following a five-year period of residence, then that new Canadian should be on a par with older Canadians in obtaining the old age assistance or old age security.
I wish to speak briefly on unemployment assistance and unemployment insurance. I say that it is always a problem with us because in Canada we are beset with problems that arise out of our geography and our weather so we do have regional and seasonal unemployment. This being so, I look forward to the measures which will be forthcoming concerning the sharing of unemployment assistance between the provinces and the dominion and also better unemployment insurance legislation.
Finally, as to health insurance: what is proposed by the government would absorb something like 50 per cent of the cost of hospitalization provided we can obtain the co-operation of more than half the provinces and provided those provinces represent more than half of the population of the nation. Now, the reason for the optimism as to the success of those proposals I think lies in the fact that a recent public opinion survey indicates


more than two-thirds of the people of Canada are in favour of the government's proposals.
At the moment there are considerable health services in this nation of ours handled by public authorities. The indigents in the lower income groups receive a scattered type of health service throughout the country from governments at provincial levels. In 1952 there were limited schemes of health service for indigents in both Ontario and Nova Scotia. One cannot fail to note that according to the 1952 figures there was spent $9.96 per person in Ontario, and $10.84 per person in Nova Scotia.
However, turning to the western provinces, we find that services are much better. In the first place the western provinces had in force in 1952 more comprehensive programs than did Ontario or Nova Scotia. They spent anywhere from $50 to $75 per capita in this field. When I think of the great province of Ontario and the great province of Quebec! Those figures are an indictment against the province of Ontario in particular. Here, in central Canada, we have the great basic manufacturing industries, and yet we have this disparity as to the treatment in health services. This is a basic reason for proceeding with the first stage of a health insurance scheme now, namely nationwide hospitalization.
There are other inequities that we could mention. Hospital plans are to be considered. These plans for hospital services are operative in the middle and upper income groups principally. Private plans cover less than 50 per cent of the population, and this rate of coverage does not proceed at more than a snail's pace. In fact, I think the members of this chamber should be indebted for the research and the publications of Dr. Malcolm Taylor and also for the republication of summaries of his studies in this field of health insurance.
It is estimated that if the private plans were allowed to proceed with their coverage efforts it would take until the year 2000 to cover the whole of the Canadian population for hospital service under the auspices of private plans. Speaking personally, I say this is the mid-twentieth century which belongs to Canada, and it is unthinkable that we in this chamber should have to wait that length of time. Therefore, I see looming, the only way, public enterprise in the field of health insurance and particularly in the field of hospital insurance.
In the recent speech of Dr. Taylor before a national association a good analysis was given of many matters in relation to health insurance, and this was reviewed in the Toronto Daily Star editorial columns too. It

was pointed out that the cost of administering the private hospital plans has proved to be greatly in excess of the charges experienced by the western provinces in their publicly controlled hospital plans. These are matters which we may well consider at this time as we watch the progress made by the government in the matter of its proposals to the provinces. We should consider also the British post-war experience in the field of health insurance. We know that the British government has had a lower cost per capita in the field of health than we have had in Canada, and in the United Kingdom they have an over-all health insurance plan in force. I think we should consider this as a safe guide as we in this young nation follow the experience of the British authorities.
It is noteworthy also that last year the medical authorities of the United Kingdom visited the Canadian Medical Association in Canada and gave every assurance to Canadian medical men that health insurance was something of which they approved in the United Kingdom. It was also discussed this year at the Canadian Medical Association convention and now we see in the daily press that the Canadian medical men endorsed in convention assembled the current proposals as outlined by the government. I would just say this too. We seem to be well supplied with doctors in Canada. The national average is one doctor for every 989 people. In Ontario, we have one doctor for 874 people; in British Columbia, one for every 866 people; in Quebec, one for every 1,012 people; ind in Saskatchewan, one for every 1,288 people. I believe these to be 1951 figures, but they do indicate that if Saskatchewan can implement a hospital scheme with one doctor for every 1,288 people, surely central Canada can respond to the proposals of the government with safety.
However there is one slight reservation I have, and that has to do with our hospital resources. I find that 1953 figures disclose British Columbia operates with hospitals to the extent of 88.9 per cent of normal; Ontario operates with a figure of 67 per cent of normal; Quebec has a figure of 56.2 per cent; and Saskatchewan 87 per cent of normal.
It may be that the government should reconsider its policy of grants in aid of hospital construction, but before doing so I should like to hear from the minister, on his estimates, let us say, as to the state of hospital construction following these figures of 1953. It might be desirable to increase the grants to the provinces to the end that we might have a higher percentage across

As I conclude, may I say this as to the question of the motion of non-confidence brought against the government on moral rather than on legal grounds? Abroad we must consider the morality of federalism which is the dominating keynote of the NATO negotiations in these days of competitive coexistence. Through NATO, for Her Majesty the Queen and the commonwealth, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is seeking to marshal the forces of Americanism, Europeanism and Canadianism. This is an expanded partnership which will bring much good to the western world and, yes, to the world at large. There is the spirit of what Sir John A. Now, finally let me just speak about what I call the morality of federalism at home. The keynote of federalism at home, the keynote of the spirit of the grand design of confederation, is indeed national unity and not disunity. I for one am greatly put out that the great Conservative party of the past bases its activities in this year, 1956, on the mobilization of discontent, as outlined in the beginning of my speech. I say that on this side of the house we stand for matters which promote federalism in confederation and which promote in particular our national development, dominion-provincial reallotment of tax revenues, better old age pensions, better unemployment relief and insurance. Finally, we hope that in that way we shall attain for this nation health insurance. These things the people of Canada elect, and I do not think that we should elect for an election and play politics.

I think it would be only right if at this time we had a little review of what has gone on over the past few years in the matter of mortgage money for new homes in Canada.
Under the operation of the act prior to 1953 most of the mortgage money for new N.H.A. homes was supplied by mortgage companies and by the insurance companies of Canada with the government lending to these institutions 25 per cent of the money that was needed. The insurance and mortgage companies made a little bit on this 25 per cent in that they were able to obtain a higher rate from the purchaser than they had to

pay the government for this share of the money. However, the time came when the investment houses of Canada felt they had invested a sufficiently large share of their capital assets in housing and henceforth they would have to limit their investments in new housing to the percentage they felt was safe to have invested in housing and that any new money they would have available for this purpose would consist only in the natural growth of the percentage in terms of dollars in line with the growth of the companies and with the repayments of the loans that had already been made.
The government had ample warning of this and looked around for other means of obtaining mortgage money and they decided to call on the chartered banks of Canada. When they did call on the chartered banks of Canada, however, they decided to supply no longer 25 per cent of the needed money and ever since that amendment to the National Housing Act the federal government has not supplied 25 per cent of the capital needs for new housing. The chartered banks of Canada, some of them rather reluctantly, entered the field of housing and on the whole I think perhaps all hon. members will agree that the chartered banks of Canada have done a significant service to the Canadian people. Many suburban areas in Canada which hitherto had been unable to lay their hands on N.H.A. mortgage funds were able to undertake housing programs because of the existence of chartered banks branches in the suburban areas simply because the banks proved themselves more accommodating and a little more willing to move into the suburban areas than the insurance companies had been. However, even the chartered banks, like the insurance companies before them, decided it would be safe for them to invest a certain specified percentage of their assets in housing.
The time has now arrived-and it arrived for some of the banks as early as six months ago-when that percentage allotment has been used up and last new year the banks gave warning to the government that henceforth their investments in new housing would be limited to the repayment on advances they had made in former years and the natural growth in the assets of the banks and to the extent that the percentage in the assets each year would be able to make more money available to them. The government had plenty of warning and yet the Minister of Public Works on January 19 saw fit to deny any knowledge of the impending shortage of mortgage money. As late as June 21, even the Minister of Finance denied that he had had several months of warning.
I feel the Minister of Finance, if indeed he is a minister of finance, had ample warning;

One of the recommendations I have made from time to time is that the government re-enter the field, at least to the extent of supplying 25 per cent of this money, as they did before the chartered banks were brought into the picture. I cannot blame the insurance companies of Canada, nor can I blame the chartered banks of Canada. After all, for many years during the hungry thirties we did not build any new homes in Canada, and yet the population grew. During the war housebuilding came to an end, so that at the end of the war there were from half a million to a million homes badly needed. We have never yet caught up.
The Minister of Public Works pointed out that last year we built some 50,000 more homes than new family units were formed. Another reason why I feel that I at least have lost confidence in one minister of this government and that an election should be called-and I am again coming back to the same minister-is the policy he pursues.

speechtext:
I am afraid that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will not have any room to be a candidate in my riding because already I hear that the Minister of National Defence has selected that riding. If that should be the case, might I inform him that he may find a bunch of shipwrecked people in the slums of Vancouver centre whose vote he can buy at $5 a piece, which the Liberal party has always bought ever since they robbed Arnold Webster of that seat in 1935, and that in my riding the Minister of National Defence will be unable to win an election on that basis. There will be a thousand volunteer workers who will be worth more than $100,000 of Liberal bribe money any day.
Now I should like to come back to the Minister of Public Works. A year ago, Mr. Speaker, you will remember, we held up the prorogation or the adjournment of this house on the subject of federal aid to universities. That was sufficient cause to hold up the adjournment. That subject was worthy by itself. However, on the day following, as a result of our holding up this house for one more day, the member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) was able to ask the Minister of Public Works concerning the sale of veterans' houses to the veterans in Regina. When I got home after the adjournment of the house I found that there were also hundreds of people in


the lower mainland who were very much interested in this subject. When the minister on that day-I believe it was July 29- replied to the member for Regina City, his reply was to the effect that the government, in selling these homes to veterans, was not planning on making any money. The plan was only to break even, but the government was not planning on making any money from the veterans.
I had noticed that the member for Regina City asked, "Why is it that the veterans of Regina are being asked to pay for these houses almost as much as the houses originally cost? When I came back to the lower mainland, I found that the veterans there in the Renfrew Heights subdivision were being asked to pay, not a little less than these houses cost, not what these houses cost, but much more than these houses cost. The Liberals who were at the mass meeting in Renfrew Heights repeated the minister's answer, "We are not making any money on these veterans' houses." However, I feel that the government may not be planning on making any money on these veterans' homes over the nation as a whole, but that is not interfering with the government's plans to make these veterans in this area and living in those homes make up the losses that the government will have to accept in other of the 92 cities of Canada.
The veterans in Renfrew Heights in Vancouver are being asked to pay thousands of dollars more for these homes than these homes cost, in order to help the government out of the losses it is experiencing on homes in other Canadian cities. That was one statement I made at one time at this mass meeting, and one statement that the government has never yet officially denied. The only answer government spokemen had at the meetings was that the veterans are buying these homes. I can list my home for sale, which is perhaps worth $15,000, and I can sell it for $30,000. As long as I am willing to take a $10 down payment, I can always find a fish who will buy that home and obligate himself and his descendants after him to pay interest for all eternity. The reason why the veterans are buying the homes is that they cannot resist buying them. The down payments are so low and, despite the denials of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials, there is pressure exerted upon them to purchase these homes. They finally yield and buy these homes, simply because they have not the necessary down payment to go on the market and buy themselves decent homes at market values.
I feel that the Minister of Public Works should reassess the whole situation, and from

the Vancouver people he should take only such money as these homes in Vancouver cost. It the government has made a blunder and perhaps lost a thousand homes in a swamp somewhere in northern Ontario, the veterans in Renfrew Heights should not be asked to foot the bill for them in the cost of their homes.
Then, coming back to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), I am afraid time will not permit me to deal with everything I should like to concerning that minister.

I am very glad to be able to represent such a progressive community as Burnaby in the House of Commons. We have there a voluntary organization known as the New Vista housing society, of which the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) is a permanent member of the board of directors. This organization collects money throughout the municipality of 80,000 people for the purpose of building low rent housing for senior citizens and other people of equally low income. They obtain from the Social Credit government of the province, reactionary as it is, formerly a Liberal-Conservative coalition government almost as reactionary, a grant of one-third of the capital cost. Through tag days, service organizations and what-have-you the people raise as much money as they can. They receive one-third of the cost from the provincial government. But then does the federal government come along through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and make a grant? Oh no. It would be horrible to help our senior citizens and people on low incomes. We could not afford to do that. They will grant them a mortgage which has to be repaid with interest over a period of 30, 40 or I believe in some cases even 50 years.'
When one looks at the resources of the various levels of government in Canada, I feel it is high time that the municipal government and the provincial government should be relieved of costs such as these. If they are not relieved, then their contribution should at least be matched by an equal contribution by the federal government. These old age pensioners are very fortunate in comparison to those who must rent on the open market. However, even to them $25 a month is a very large share of their income indeed to have to pay for rent. Why? In order to repay the mortgage held by the federal government.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) gets considerable publicity back home with his announcements each time the
